# Package Notes {#sec-93-package-notes}



What this book was built against, where it deviates from the released packages,
and why. Everything here is a deliberate choice rather than an accident of
whatever happened to be installed.

## The build environment


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Item                 |Version |
|:--------------------|:-------|
|R                    |4.6.1   |
|PortfolioAnalytics   |2.1.2   |
|PerformanceAnalytics |2.1.0   |
|tidyfinance          |0.8.0   |
|CVXR                 |1.9.2   |
|xts                  |0.14.2  |
|packages pinned      |299     |


:::
:::


The complete set is in `renv.lock`. To reproduce the book exactly:

```r
renv::restore()
quarto::quarto_render()
```

## Why PortfolioAnalytics is pinned to the CRAN release

The development version on GitHub is usually ahead of CRAN, sometimes by
several months and several bug fixes. This book nonetheless builds against the
**CRAN release**, for one reason: you install from CRAN, and a book that only
runs against an unreleased commit is not reproducible for its readers.

The cost is that a fix landing upstream in, say, July does not reach the book
until the next CRAN release. Where that gap matters, it is named in the chapter
that hits it.

The exception is a patch that this book itself contributes. While such a patch
is under review, the lockfile points at a branch of a fork; once merged and
released, it points back at CRAN. Any patch currently in that state is listed
below.

### Patches in flight

The book's own pull requests against `braverock/PortfolioAnalytics` stand as
follows at the time of writing (November 2026). Two small ones were merged on
19 September 2026: #60, a legend that `chart.EfficientFrontierCompare()` failed
to draw with `guideline = FALSE`, and #61, a test that `ROI` masked in a suite
run. Neither is needed by the book. The four that the book depends on are
**open**, and the lockfile therefore points at the fork branch
`book-integration`, which carries all four; once they are merged and released,
it points back at CRAN.

**Pinned.** Every fix below either restores an answer that was wrong or turns a
silent `NA` into a message. None of them makes a call fail that used to succeed,
which is why the book builds against them.

| Pull request | What it fixes | Where it bites |
|---|---|---|
| #55 | `full_investment` is encoded as two opposing inequalities, which makes the active set rank deficient; the solver fails and `NA` weights are returned without a message | @sec-25-backtesting-implementation |
| #56 | `maxSR` is recovered from `match.call()`, so it only works when written as a literal `TRUE`; driving it from a variable fails outright | @sec-13-solvers-implementation |
| #57 | `maxSR` discards a mean supplied through `momentFUN`, so the "maximum Sharpe" answer is not the maximum Sharpe answer | @sec-09-mean-variance-application, @sec-13-solvers-implementation |
| #58 | a rebalancing period whose solver fails is reported, with what went wrong, instead of vanishing from the result | @sec-25-backtesting-implementation |

A fifth, #59, adds an opt-in override to `statistical.factor.model()`'s
fewer-observations-than-assets check; it is open too but not pinned, because
no chapter needs it.

**Not fixed anywhere.** Position limits and `maxSR` under a turnover
constraint are accepted and then dropped, so the returned portfolio violates
what was asked for. On the build this book pins, a position limit (`max_pos`)
on ROI's quadratic path is dropped without a message: no error, no warning, and
the unconstrained weights come back, exactly as on the CRAN release. ROI honors
the limit only on its two mixed-integer paths, maximum return and minimum
expected shortfall, which it hands to `Rglpk`. Refusing the quadratic call would
be the honest fix, but it breaks code that runs today; no patch for it exists
upstream or on the fork, and this book documents the behavior instead.
@sec-12-constraints-implementation and @sec-92-solver-matrix measure it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|fact                       |value   |
|:--------------------------|:-------|
|version string             |2.1.2   |
|build actually loaded      |patched |
|what the lockfile restores |GitHub  |


:::
:::


::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The two builds share a version string.** Both call themselves 2.1.2, so
`packageVersion()` cannot tell them apart and neither can `renv`. The patched
build is identified by a formal argument the patch adds, which is what
`tidyaa_pa_patched()` in `R/_common.R` checks; a render against the unpatched
build emits a warning rather than silently producing different numbers.

`renv.lock` pins the patched build by commit, so `renv::restore()` installs it
and no extra step is needed. Should the pin ever revert to CRAN, the warning is
how you find out.
:::

### Upstream issues this book documents

These are live limitations, not bugs the book works around silently. Each is
taught in the chapter where it bites.

| Issue | Effect | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| [#45](https://github.com/braverock/PortfolioAnalytics/issues/45) | `optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` reports nothing when a solver fails in a period | @sec-25-backtesting-implementation |
| [#43](https://github.com/braverock/PortfolioAnalytics/issues/43) | No control over the parallelisation level in rolling optimization | @sec-14-risk-based-allocation-implementation |
| [#51](https://github.com/braverock/PortfolioAnalytics/issues/51) | CSM objective unavailable to the metaheuristic solvers | @sec-10-risk-measures-implementation |

## Version holds

Not every available update is taken. Where the book stays behind, the reason is
recorded here rather than left as an accident.

| Package | Pinned at | Available | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `clarabel` | 0.11.2 | 0.11.3 | No binary is published for R 4.6 yet, and `clarabel` compiles from Rust rather than C, so building from source needs a `cargo` toolchain that Rtools does not provide. 0.11.2 is a working CVXR backend; revisit once a binary appears. |

`zoo` moved to 1.9-0 with the R 4.6 upgrade. That is a major version directly
underneath `xts`, which every chapter depends on, so it is worth stating
explicitly: `xts` 0.14.2 loads and passes against it, and no chapter has yet
exercised the combination in anger. If a time-series operation behaves oddly,
this pairing is the first place to look.

## The two packages that do not come from CRAN

Everything the book uses installs from CRAN with one deliberate exception each
side of the boundary.

`tidypm` is the companion package. It is not on CRAN and is not meant to be
installed from there; it holds the modeled market and the machinery
`PortfolioAnalytics` does not cover.

`uncertaintymeasures` [@stoeckl-uncertaintymeasures] implements the
turbulence-based uncertainty measures used in @sec-05-factor-models-application, and the
Garlappi-Uppal-Wang multi-prior adjustment [@garlappi2007] used in
@sec-28-robustness-application. It installs from GitHub:

```r
renv::install("sstoeckl/uncertaintymeasures")
```

A GitHub dependency is a reproducibility cost, and it is worth being explicit
about who pays it. The book renders the excursus live rather than from a stored
figure, so a reader who wants to rebuild that section needs the package; a
reader who only wants the rest does not. The alternative — printing a frozen
image and disabling the code — would have shown the result while hiding the one
thing worth showing, which is how it is computed.

## Which package to reach for

Four packages overlap across data, estimation and evaluation, and the obvious
guess is wrong at least once. The division used throughout:

| Job | Package | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Moments, distributions, drawdowns, alphas and betas, active-management measures, exploratory charts | `PerformanceAnalytics` | On CRAN since 2007 with a stable interface, and already a hard dependency. It covers more than most readers realize: `CAPM.beta.bull()` and `CAPM.beta.bear()` give conditional betas in one call, `table.DownsideRisk()` and `table.Distributions()` replace a page of hand-written summaries. |
| Staying in tibbles across that boundary | `tidyquant` | `tq_performance()` wraps the above and returns a tibble. |
| Fetching data nobody else wraps — JKP factors, Goyal–Welch predictors, WRDS and its credential-free substitutes | `tidyfinance` | Nothing else offers these. **Used for data access only, never for estimation:** it is pre-1.0 and its estimation interfaces are still moving, which is a poor foundation for a book that has to keep rendering. |
| Optimization | `PortfolioAnalytics` | The subject of the book. |

Written by hand only where none of the four has the function. Rolling betas as a
*table* are one such case: `PerformanceAnalytics` charts them through
`chart.RollingRegression()` but returns nothing, so the book composes
`zoo::rollapply()` with `CAPM.beta()`. Three visible lines that will not move
beat one call that might.

## Notes on the snapshot

Most of `renv.lock` resolves from CRAN, but three entries do not, and each
needs a word.

`uncertaintymeasures` and `PortfolioAnalytics` are both recorded as GitHub
sources with commit hashes, so they restore exactly:

| Package | Pinned at |
|---|---|
| `PortfolioAnalytics` | `` sstoeckl/PortfolioAnalytics@2a4dd910 ``, branch `` book-integration `` |
| `uncertaintymeasures` | `` sstoeckl/uncertaintymeasures@d822c2f5 `` |

`tidypm` is the one entry that does not resolve from a network location. It is
recorded as a **local** source at `../tidypm`, because the companion package is
a sibling directory rather than a published one, so restoring it needs that
directory to be present.

```r
renv::restore()
source("R/_common.R")   # warns if the PortfolioAnalytics patch did not take
```

## R version

The book targets R 4.6.1.

The companion package `tidypm` deliberately declares a lower floor
(`R (>= 4.2)`). The book's lockfile pins a *build* environment; the package
states what a *reader* needs. These are different constraints and there is no
reason to make readers follow the build.
